faqs.question: What is the hardest Halloween tongue twister?
faqs.answer: Of the 35 on this page, try "The sixth thief's fifth thimble thrice slipped": it stacks the k-s-th ending of "sixth" against "fifth" and "thrice". For p and b, "Pumpkin bumpkin, bumpkin pumpkin, pumpkin bumpkin bumps" is the one that trips adults.

faqs.question: What's a good Halloween tongue twister for a 4-year-old?
faqs.answer: Short p and b lines such as "Big bat, pink pot" work best, because US children usually master p and b before age 3. Say it slowly together a couple of times and skip the timer.

faqs.question: Why does my 5-year-old say "free" instead of "three"?
faqs.answer: That is normal. A 2020 review covering 18,907 US children found the "thin" sound is mastered by 90% of children only between 6;0 and 6;11 (years;months), making it the last English consonant to arrive.

faqs.question: How do you score a say-it-three-times-fast game?
faqs.answer: Start each turn on 10 points, take off 1 for every slip, stall or restart, and add 2 for finishing all three repetitions in under 6 seconds (10 seconds for ages 4–6). Adult lines score double, and 3 rounds decide the winner.

faqs.question: Do tongue twisters help with English pronunciation?
faqs.answer: They help once you can hear the difference between the two sounds, so practise slowly and record yourself. The th set matters most for many learners, because th-type sounds appear in only 43 of the 566 languages sampled by the World Atlas of Language Structures.

faqs.question: Are tongue twisters used in speech therapy?
faqs.answer: Therapists build a sound up from syllables to words, phrases and sentences, so a twister belongs at the sentence end of practice. If your child sees a speech-language pathologist, ask which sound to work on before playing anything timed.

faqs.question: Did Guinness World Records name a hardest tongue twister?
faqs.answer: The sheikh's-sheep line is often described as a Guinness entry, but we found no record page for it on guinnessworldrecords.com on 14 October 2026. Treat that claim as unverified until Guinness publishes one.

faqs.question: How do I write my own Halloween tongue twister?
faqs.answer: Pick two sounds made in nearly the same place, such as s and sh, keep the vowels steady and swap only the first consonant of each word. Five to ten words is plenty; longer lines turn into a memory test.

faqs.question: Why do I slip on a tongue twister even when I say it in my head?
faqs.answer: Speech is planned before it is spoken, and that plan can scramble sounds that share most of their features. A 2023 brain-imaging study used silently recited twisters for that reason, after a 28-person pilot in which standard twisters drew errors 23% of the time.

faqs.question: Can I send a tongue twister to someone who lives far away?
faqs.answer: Yes. The premium SubhSandesh Halloween page takes a voice note of up to 60 seconds, enough to record one twister three times fast; the regular card has no audio, so the twister goes in the letter.

# Halloween Tongue Twisters for Kids and Adults: 35 Sorted by Sound

Here are 35 original Halloween tongue twisters, sorted by the sound they train (s/sh, p/b, w/wh/v, r/l and th) and by level: short lines for ages 4–6, longer ones for ages 7–10 and "impossible" ones for adults. A say-it-three-times-fast scoring game follows, ready for Halloween night (Saturday 31 October 2026; Sunday 31 October 2027).

No line runs past a dozen words, since phones account for 48.3% of SubhSandesh page opens (27,725 of 57,456 views). Spoken lines invite replays, and a SubhSandesh page averages 11.1 views. After the lists: why these sounds collide, the age children master each, help for English learners, and cases to avoid the game.

## What is a tongue twister, and why is it hard to say fast?

A tongue twister is a phrase built from words that share most of their sounds but swap one, so the mouth must switch between near-identical movements at speed. Slowly it is easy; three times fast, the planned sounds trade places.

Psycholinguists use twisters as a lab tool for exactly that reason; a 1999 paper in *Language and Speech* is titled "The 'tongue twister' paradigm as a technique for studying phonological encoding". In a review in *Psychological Bulletin*, Daniel Acheson and Maryellen MacDonald note that [over 80% of exchange-type speech slips involve the consonant at the start of a syllable](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC3000524), and that reading twisters aloud and recalling them produce the same errors. So the lines below keep vowels steady and swap first consonants.

Slips start before any sound comes out. In a [2023 study in *Neurobiology of Language*](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10205072), Alex Teghipco and colleagues at UC Irvine report a pilot with 28 adults in which standard twisters drew errors 23% of the time, and they review brain-scan evidence of near-slips being caught even on trials spoken correctly.

## 35 original Halloween tongue twisters, by sound and age

All 35 are new. Each set has 2 short lines for ages 4–6, 3 for ages 7–10 and 2 adult "impossible" lines; go slow before going fast.

### 1. S and SH: ghost-sheet twisters (7 lines)

These train the hiss of s against the hush of sh, made with the tongue in almost the same spot. Mid-word switches like "sheet-ghosts" are the trap.

- Ages 4–6: Six shy sheets.
- Ages 4–6: She sews spooky socks.
- Ages 7–10: Sheila's shadow shushes six silly spiders.
- Ages 7–10: Seven shivering skeletons share one shoe.
- Ages 7–10: Sasha's spooky shop sells short shiny shrouds.
- Adults: Sixty-six sheet-ghosts shushed the sheriff's seasick sister.
- Adults: Swiss witch Sasha's shabby sash slips, so she switches sashes.

### 2. P and B: pumpkin-patch twisters (7 lines)

These train the puff of air that separates p from b, since both close the lips and only the voice changes. A paper strip held at your lips flutters on p, not on b.

- Ages 4–6: Big bat, pink pot.
- Ages 4–6: Bob's purple pumpkin pops.
- Ages 7–10: Pete's plump pumpkin bumped Bess's bent broom.
- Ages 7–10: Bea's bat bounced Pip's paper pumpkin back.
- Ages 7–10: Paul's pumpkin path passes Bill's broken barn.
- Adults: Pumpkin bumpkin, bumpkin pumpkin, pumpkin bumpkin bumps.
- Adults: Brett's bat-proof pumpkin box blocks Pip's pumpkin-proof bat box.

### 3. W, WH and V: werewolf-and-vampire twisters (7 lines)

These train rounded lips for w and wh against top teeth on the lower lip for v. Many English learners merge this pair, so set 3 doubles as an accent drill.

- Ages 4–6: Wet webs, wide wings.
- Ages 4–6: Vicky's vampire waves.
- Ages 7–10: Willow's wobbly werewolf wants warm waffles.
- Ages 7–10: Where were the werewolf's wet wellies?
- Ages 7–10: A vampire with velvet wings visits Will's village.
- Adults: Very wary vampires wave while wolves weave west.
- Adults: Which way would weary vampires walk while wet werewolves wait?

### 4. R and L: lantern twisters (7 lines)

These train the tongue tip touching the ridge behind the teeth for l against the curled r, which touches nothing. In US data l is usually mastered by age 4 and r a year later, so a 5-year-old saying "wed" for "red" is on schedule.

- Ages 4–6: Lily's red lantern.
- Ages 4–6: Rory rolls a lolly.
- Ages 7–10: Larry's rattling lantern really lights the lonely road.
- Ages 7–10: Little Rita's rubber lizard lost its lolly.
- Ages 7–10: Roll the round lantern, leave the long rake.
- Adults: The rural ruler's lurid lantern lured three rowdy wraiths.
- Adults: Rarely do lurking werewolves really roll left.

### 5. TH: foggy-night twisters (7 lines)

These train the tongue tip between the teeth for th, the last English consonant US children master, usually between ages 6 and 7. A 5-year-old saying "free fin ghosts" is not making a mistake worth correcting.

- Ages 4–6: Three thin ghosts.
- Ages 4–6: This thing thumps.
- Ages 7–10: Thirty thirsty thieves thought the thunder was a ghost.
- Ages 7–10: Theo threw the thimble through the thorny thicket.
- Ages 7–10: The thick fog thinned, then thickened, then thinned.
- Adults: The thirty-third ghost thought the thirty-fourth ghost's theme was thin.
- Adults: The sixth thief's fifth thimble thrice slipped.

## The say-it-three-times-fast scoring game

Each player picks a twister at their level and says it three times without pausing while a judge times them. It works for 2 to 12 players.

- **Start each turn on 10 points.**
- **Lose 1 point** for every swapped sound, stall or restart; the judge counts and the room can appeal once.
- **Gain 2 points** for finishing all three in under 6 seconds (ages 4–6 get 10 seconds).
- **Double the turn score** on an adult "impossible" line; a score below zero counts as zero.
- **Laughing mid-line** costs 1 point, not the turn.
- **Tie-break whisper round:** both players whisper one line three times. Slips are planned before sound leaves the mouth (Teghipco's team studied silent recitation), so whispering is no escape.

Play 3 rounds; the highest total wins. Let ages 4–6 say their line twice slowly before the timer starts, because slow accuracy comes first.

## Which tongue twister level suits which age?

The table matches each sound group to the age by which 90% of US children say it correctly, from a [2020 review of 15 studies covering 18,907 children](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33181047) by Kathryn Crowe and Sharynne McLeod. Ages are years;months.

| Sound group | Mastered by 90% of US children | Start scoring at | Lines here |
|---|---|---|---|
| P and B | 2;0–2;11 | Ages 4–6 | 7 |
| S and SH | 4;0–4;11 | Ages 4–6 | 7 |
| W, WH and V | w 2;0–2;11, v 4;0–4;11 | Ages 4–6 | 7 |
| R and L | l 4;0–4;11, r 5;0–5;11 | Ages 6+ | 7 |
| TH | "this" 5;0–5;11, "thin" 6;0–6;11 | Ages 7+ | 7 |

So p/b twisters suit the youngest players; leave th unscored until about 7.

## Halloween tongue twisters for English learners

English th is rare worldwide. Ian Maddieson's chapter in the World Atlas of Language Structures finds th-type sounds in [only 43 of 566 sampled languages, or 7.6%](https://wals.info/chapter/19), so many learners never needed the tongue-between-teeth position before English.

Learners should score accuracy, not speed: say each line slowly 3 times, record it, and compare it with a fluent speaker.

- **Start with set 5** if "think" comes out as "tink" or "sink".
- **Use set 3** if "vampire" and "wampire" sound the same to you.
- **Use set 4** if your first language has one sound where English has r and l.

## Can tongue twisters help with speech therapy?

Speech-language pathologists move a target sound from syllables to words, phrases and sentences, says the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association's [practice portal on speech sound disorders](https://www.asha.org/practice-portal/clinical-topics/articulation-and-phonology/). A tongue twister is a sentence-level drill, so it belongs near the end of that sequence, not the start.

Speech sound difficulties are common: ASHA cites estimates of 2.1%–23% of 4- to 6-year-olds, and 3.6% of 8-year-olds with persistent ones. A child in therapy should use the set their therapist picks, untimed.

## Is "the sixth sick sheikh's sixth sheep's sick" a Guinness record?

"The sixth sick sheikh's sixth sheep's sick" is widely repeated online as the Guinness World Records' hardest English tongue twister. We found no record page for it on guinnessworldrecords.com when we checked on 14 October 2026, so treat the claim as unverified.

Record or not, its 7 words are genuinely hard: they pack s, sh and the k-s-th cluster ending "sixth" twice, the ending our last th line borrows.

## Sending a recorded tongue twister to one person

Neither SubhSandesh Halloween page runs a group game; each greets a single recipient. They suit the grandparent, cousin or best friend missing from your table.

[A premium Halloween greeting that plays your recorded voice](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) accepts a clip of 60 seconds at most, room for a child to try one twister three times and giggle after; the spirit radio plays it. Allow roughly 10 minutes to build it, add a dozen photos at most, and set an unlock time if it should open only on 31 October; kids mode hides the No button.

[The haunted-house Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) carries no audio, so write the twister in the flashlit letter and let its trickiest word glow on the carved pumpkin. Building it needs around 5 minutes and up to six photos, and its Kids tone avoids gore and jump scares. A password is sensible if a child's voice is involved, and 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators set one (2,000 of 5,199); other occasions are in [the full SubhSandesh template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates).

## When to skip the tongue twister game

Timed twisters suit most players, but not all. Change or drop the game in these 4 cases:

- **A child who stutters or is in speech therapy.** A stopwatch adds pressure; check with their therapist first.
- **Brand-new English speakers.** Speed rewards native speakers; score accuracy only.
- **Children under 4.** Use the short p/b lines as call-and-repeat with no scoring.
- **A class of 20 or more.** Our pages greet one named person, so print these lists for a classroom.

## Sources

- Acheson and MacDonald (2009), Psychological Bulletin (author manuscript).
- Teghipco, Okada, Murphy and Hickok (2023), Neurobiology of Language, 8 March 2023.
- Crowe and McLeod (2020), American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology (abstract only).
- Maddieson (2013), WALS Online chapter 19.
- ASHA Practice Portal, Speech Sound Disorders: Articulation and Phonology (undated).

Crowe & McLeod, 'Children's English Consonant Acquisition in the United States: A Review', American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology 2020 (ASHA), ABSTRACT ONLY read: 15 studies, 18,907 children; /b n m p h w d/ by 2;0-2;11, /g k f t ŋ j/ by 3;0-3;11, /v dʒ s tʃ l ʃ z/ by 4;0-4;11, /ɹ ð ʒ/ by 5;0-5;11, /θ/ by 6;0-6;11 (90% criterion); most consonants by 5;0.

Ian Maddieson, 'Presence of Uncommon Consonants', WALS Online chapter 19 (Max Planck, 2013 edition): dental/alveolar non-sibilant fricatives ('th' sounds) occur in just 43 (7.6%) of the 566 languages surveyed, including Modern Greek, Albanian, Spanish and English.

ASHA Practice Portal, Speech Sound Disorders: Articulation and Phonology (undated, cited as n.d.): treatment generalization proceeds through syllables, words, phrases/sentences, conversation; speech motor chaining progression syllables > monosyllabic words > multisyllabic words > phrases > self-generated sentences; 2.1%-23% of 4- to 6-year-olds estimated to have SSDs; 3.6% of 8-year-olds persistent SSDs (Wren et al., 2016). ASHA does not mention tongue twisters; the post does not claim it does.
